title: This Norwegian village is one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. How can its people save it?
summary:

As glaciers melt and permafrost thaws, Longyearbyen, on the remote Arctic islands of Svalbard, faces climate-induced problems from tap water to housebuilding to landslides Heavy metals make Norwegian village’s tap water toxic Supported by About this content Karen McVeigh in Longyearbyen, Norway Wed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n a rugged mountain plateau of snow-dusted rocks, in the remote archipelago of Svalbard, a glaciologist, Andy Hodson, points out the “ears” of ice, white against the rock, that gave Foxfonna glacier its name, after the arctic fox. The small glacier, on a mountain 8 miles (15km) outside the Norwegian village of Longyearbyen, is a popular summer hike for tourists who come here seeking the Arctic experience. But in Svalbard, where glaciers cover 57% of the land and temperatures are rising up to seven times faster than the global average, making it one of the fastest-warming places on Earth, Foxfonna is changing rapidly. “It is slowly dying,” says Hodson, a professor at the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS). The telltale signs include a concave profile: Foxfonna is no longer accumulating snow. Precipitation here is increasingly falling as rain. Its thinning rate is between 1 and 4 metres a year, making it unrecognisable from when Hodson was last here a few years ago. Out in the fjords, on the other side of the coastal village, the large glacial fronts extending into the sea that are characteristic of the islands are melting at an even faster rate: over the past two years, 10 have retreated entirely on to land . In 2024, “things went crazy”, Hodson says, after record-high summer temperatures led to a big ice loss, of 1% , across the archipelago. It is affected by Arctic amplification – a feedback loop in which sea-ice retreat and atmospheric warming make each other worse. View image in fullscreen Andy Hodson points to Foxfonna’s concave profile, a sign that the glacier no longer accumulates snow. Photograph: K McVeigh/Guardian “Pretty much the whole island is losing ice now,” says Hodson. Longyearbyen, a scatter of brightly coloured houses, research institutes and tourist hotels at the bottom of a steep valley, lies at a latitude of 78 degrees north, the last stop in the high Arctic before the north pole. An important outpost of Arctic science, it attracts explorers, adventurers and nature lovers. The village’s 2,600 inhabitants are used to extremes: winter temperatures can drop as low as -20C (-4F) and, from late October to early March, the sun does not rise, plunging the valley into more than 100 days of darkness. View image in fullscreen Marjolaine Verret takes water samples. Photograph: Tonje Emilie Stenstad/The Guardian But they are now facing new and unsettling challenges – things that many point out should serve as a warning for other Arctic regions. Not only is snow melting faster but now the permafrost – ground that once remained frozen all year – is thawing. This is having unexpected but significant consequences. People have recently been warned not to drink from their taps due to heavy metals contained in the bedrock leaching into the village’s water supply. Instead, they now have to fill up containers from a central tank of filtered water in the village’s supermarket, while the municipality investigates and works out what to do in the long term. The thaw has also caused landslides, damaged foundations and cracked walls, rendering some homes uninhabitable and threatening the long-term stability of other buildings. As a consequence, there are no longer enough homes for the number of people who need them. The authorities in Longyearbyen have been forced to learn lessons, acclimatise and try to adapt to the changing conditions.
